Reaches `#` state or a sibling method \u001a private method.\r\n181: 2. Recursive spine or composition of leaves (`solve`, `isolate`, `prove`, chaining, relational join), even if pure \u001a private method.\r\n183: 4. Defining engine internals remain methods when extraction would hollow the class into a thin delegate.\r\n184: \r\n185: Extract pure leaves aggressively; keep the class's actual behavior.\r\n186: \r\n187: ## Class order\r\n188: \r\n189: 1. `#` private fields: context, options, state/result, child managers.\r\n190: 2. Change a fence, change the transcription beside it.\r\n73: - `integration.test.ts` is a reserved filename at any level. It names a scope rather than a module,\r\n74:   so the mirror rule does not reach it; its scope is the directory it sits in.\r\n75: - An integration test is an end-to-end test: it composes the package's own features and drives them\r\n76:   together, through the public API, with no part of the system under test replaced.\r\n77: - Scope it by where the composition happens. `tests/integration.test.ts` drives features **across**\r\n78:   environments - core through server, core through browser, one environment's output consumed by\r\n79:   another. A nested `tests/src/<environment>/integration.test.ts` drives features **within** that one\r\n80:   environment.\r\n81: - Do not put a packaging, install, or distribution check in an integration test. What the tarball\r\n82:   contains is a different question from whether the features compose.\r\n83: - A test the mirror rule flags is a misplaced test until its placement is checked. Move it to the\r\n84:   location its scope names. Widen the rule only when that check shows the test already sits at the\r\n85:   location its scope names and the rule's population omits a module this ruleset mandates, and then\r\n86:   widen the population rather than admitting the individual case.\r\n87: - A nested `tests/{src,app}/<environment>/**/integration.test.ts` runs in that environment's project,\r\n88:   whose existing glob collects it exactly once. Give it a separate exact-path project entry only when\r\n89:   the proof needs different setup or a different runtime, and exclude that exact path from the\r\n90:   environment project when you do.\r\n91: \r\n92: ## Probes\r\n93: \r\n94: A probe is a throwaway instrument that settles one question. It is not a test and never ships.\r\n95: \r\n96: Route the question before writing a probe. When you can state the edit you believe is correct and the\r\n97: edit that must break with the stage it breaks at, the question is a claim for the `prove` tool the\r\n98: `probe` MCP server registers, and `.claude/rules/quality.md` \u0015 Instruments owns that rule. When the\r\n99: question carries no stated belief to falsify yet, when the subject lies outside the TypeScript a\r\n100: workspace project judges, or when the proof needs what that tool's stages do not model - a process\r\n101: tree, a listening socket, an installed package, a built entry driven as a child, or a live external\r\n102: service - write a probe.\r\n103: \r\n104: The kinds split by which tool has to see the probe:\r\n105: \r\n106: - A **type probe** is read by `tsc`, whose scoped project includes only its own environment, so it\r\n107:   lives in the source tree beside what it measures. Delete it before the unit returns; a leaked one\r\n108:   fails the `policy` plugin's placement rules, because a probe filename is not a centralized kind\r\n109:   file.\r\n110: - A **runtime probe** is collected by a Vitest project, so it lives in `tmp/probe/` and runs through\r\n111:   the `probe` project. `tmp/` is ignored by git, so no probe enters a commit by accident, and every\r\n112:   test script names its project, so no gate runs the `probe` project.\r\n113: - A **bench** is read by Vitest's benchmark mode, so it lives inside a test file as a block behind\r\n114:   the `if (import.meta.env.MODE === 'benchmark')` guard. Only the `test:bench` script collects the\r\n115:   block, test mode fails an unguarded `bench()` call loudly, and no gate runs a bench. Call `bench`\r\n116:   directly inside the guard. A `describe` inside it trips `vitest/no-conditional-tests`, and a suite\r\n117:   the guard leaves unregistered fails test mode with `No test found in suite`.\r\n118: \r\n119: Run a probe before relying on an unverified belief about behaviour: what a function returns, what a\r\n120: configuration resolves to, whether a path is reached at all. Prefer a probe to an argument whenever\r\n121: the probe is cheap.\r\n122: \r\n123: When the question is whether the difference between methods is a magnitude or negligible, write a\r\n124: guarded bench block beside the probe test and run the `test:bench` script. Declare the threshold\r\n125: before the run, read the ratio between the methods against each side's reported uncertainty, and\r\n126: record nothing below a magnitude. A settled magnitude that underwrites an implementation choice\r\n127: promotes with its test into the mirrored suite and keeps its guarded block there while that choice\r\n128: stands. A deterministic relationship promotes as an ordinary assertion, so delete the block. Never\r\n129: commit baseline output.\r\n130: \r\n131: These rules bind every probe:\r\n132: \r\n133: - **Prove the instrument can fail before trusting that it passed.** Pair it with a control drawn\r\n134:   from outside the population it covers.\r\n135: - **Promote or delete.** A probe that settles a claim becomes a test in the mirrored location that\r\n136:   proves the real source. Delete every other probe. A probe left in the suite reports on the harness\r\n137:   while reading as a test.\r\n138: - **Never commit a probe.** The ignore rule stops an accident, not a deliberate forced add, and a\r\n139:   type probe sits in tracked source with no ignore rule at all.\r\n140: \r\n141: ## Live-service tests\r\n142: \r\n143: Live external services/models are the deliberate exception to fast hermetic defaults:\r\n144: \r\n145: - Put them in the `service` project, under `tests/service/`, with `tests/setupService.ts` for setup\r\n146:   and a longer timeout. That module's presence is what registers the project, so a live proof with\r\n147:   no readiness setup is a project nothing configures.\r\n148: - `.claude/rules/workspace.md` fixes which gate runs the `service` project, and that gate is not the\r\n149:   same one in a publishing and a `private: true` workspace.\r\n150: - Warm and verify service readiness in `tests/setupService.ts`.\r\n151: - Hard-require readiness: throw loudly; never silently skip.\r\n152: - Verify service-dependent logic through that service's project, not unrelated module tests or scattered conditional skips.\r\n153: - Tune each request to the smallest input/context/output that proves one behavior without becoming brittle or expensive.\r\n154: - Prefer semantic bounded assertions over exact generated prose. Increase context/workload only when the scenario requires it.\r\n155: \r\n156: ## Expensive proofs\r\n157: \r\n158: A test that spawns a process, packs, installs, or drives a real build is a proof, not a unit test.\r\n159: \r\n160: - Give it its own Vitest project with its own setup and timeout.\r\n161: - Keep it out of the default run where the workspace has a gate that can hold it.\r\n162:   `.claude/rules/workspace.md` fixes which gate each isolated project runs from, and that placement\r\n163:   differs between a publishing and a `private: true` workspace.\r\n164: - The fixed expensive-proof projects are `distribution` and `service`.\r\n165: - A `distribution` proof reads `import.meta.env.MODE` and fails, rather than skips, on an unreachable\r\n166:   registry under `--mode release`. The publish gate invokes it that way, so a proof that skips there\r\n167:   passes the gate without ever proving the artifact installs. An ordinary local run may still skip.\r\n168: - Slow and hermetic is reason enough to isolate a proof; it need not touch an external service.\r\n169: - Where such a proof stays in a shared project, size its budget from a full contended run rather than from an isolated one. A budget that clears the isolated cost by a thin margin turns contention into a red gate reporting a timeout, which carries no diagnostic about the code and costs a full investigation to dismiss.\r\n170: \r\n171: ## Shared test infrastructure\r\n172: \r\n173: Test helpers are shared infrastructure, not local test-file clutter.\r\n174: \r\n175: `@orkestrel/test` owns the helpers every workspace repeats: the call recorder, the real delay, the JSON and async collectors, and the owned scratch directory. Import them from `@orkestrel/test`, and its Node-only helpers from `@orkestrel/test/server`. Write a helper of your own only where the package exports none for the job. The following shapes are the contract a workspace codes against, not source to copy.\r\n176: \r\n177: - For the vendored test set (`tests/setupPolicy.ts`, `tests/policy.test.ts`, and\r\n178:   `tests/config.test.ts`), keep shared helpers within that set instead of importing them from\r\n179:   `@orkestrel/test`; follow the vendored-file import law in `.claude/rules/workspace.md`.\r\n180: \r\n181: - Extract a fixture, recorder, event factory, async wait, renderer, scenario/data builder, protocol fixture, or DOM builder as soon as it could serve another test.\r\n182: - Any duplicate or near-duplicate helper is a defect; consolidate it into one general form.\r\n183: - Export every reusable helper, fixture type, factory, constant, and guard from setup files.\r\n184: - A setup file owns everything an assertion needs and nothing an assertion is: `describe`, `it`, and `expect` never appear in a `setup*.ts`.\r\n185: - Data tables and case matrices belong in a setup file at any size; test registration does not.\r\n186: - Test files import shared infrastructure rather than declaring local fixture factories.\r\n187: - Never reimplement a framework helper in tests or fixtures; import the real parser, signer, flattener, or other helper.\r\n188: - Prefer small customizable factories/stubs that seed inert data for a real scenario over repeated inline setup.\r\n189: - Helper names follow module-helper naming: `createFixtureServer`, `buildElement`, `appendItems`, `renderRows`, `waitForReady`, `extractDetail`.\r\n190: \r\n191: Place helpers by environment:\r\n192: \r\n193: - `tests/setup.ts`: host-independent; no `node:*`, DOM, `window`, or Vue.\r\n194: - `tests/setupServer.ts`: Node-only helpers and `node:fs` loaders anchored to `WORKSPACE_ROOT`.\r\n195: - `tests/setupBrowser.ts`: DOM/Vue/browser helpers and setup CSS.\r\n196: - `tests/setupStyles.ts`: CSS/style helpers and compiled cascade.\r\n197: \r\n198: ### Recorder\r\n199: \r\n200: Import `createRecorder` from `@orkestrel/test` instead of a framework spy when only calls and arguments matter. It returns:\r\n201: \r\n202: ```ts\r\n203: interface RecorderInterface<TArgs extends readonly unknown[]> {\r\n204: \treadonly calls: readonly TArgs[]\r\n205: \treadonly count: number\r\n206: \treadonly handler: (...args: TArgs) => void\r\n207: \tclear(): void\r\n208: }\r\n209: ```\r\n210: \r\n211: ### Delay\r\n212: \r\n213: Import `waitForDelay` from `@orkestrel/test`; never repeat an inline timeout promise. It waits for one host timer and defaults to `0`:\r\n214: \r\n215: ```ts\r\n216: function waitForDelay(ms?: number): Promise<void>\r\n217: ```\r\n218: \r\n219: Use it to yield, never to wait for something another process produces. A fixed delay chosen to\r\n220: outlast a child's startup is a race whose loss looks like a product defect: the test measures\r\n221: interpreter bootstrap rather than the behaviour it names, and it fails on a loaded host and passes on\r\n222: an idle one. Wait until a named condition holds instead, polling with `waitForDelay` inside a budget\r\n223: measured by `performance.now()`, and fail with the condition's own description when the budget\r\n224: expires.\r\n225: \r\n226: ### Scratch\r\n227: \r\n228: Import `createScratch` from `@orkestrel/test/server` when a proof needs real files. It allocates a temporary directory it owns, contains every path against escape, and removes the directory on `destroy`:\r\n229: \r\n230: ```ts\r\n231: interface ScratchInterface {\r\n232: \treadonly path: string\r\n233: \twrite(target: string, text: string): string\r\n234: \tread(target: string): string | undefined\r\n235: \thas(target: string): boolean\r\n236: \tnames(target?: string): readonly string[]\r\n237: \tensure(target: string): string\r\n238: \tlink(target: string, source: string): string\r\n239: \tremove(target: string): void\r\n240: \tdestroy(): void\r\n241: }\r\n242: ```\r\n243: \r\n244: ### Style primitives\r\n245: \r\n246: Browser/style setup exposes shared assertions/builders:\r\n247: \r\n248: `mount`, `render`, `build`, `readStyle`, `readToken`, `readRootToken`, `readPixels`, `parseCSSColor`, `matchesColor`, `findRule`.\r\n249: \r\n250: `findRule` proves a declaration exists in the cascade; `readStyle()` reads the resolved result.\r\n251: \r\n252: ## Browser tests\r\n253: \r\n254: Use the real browser as the system under test:\r\n255: \r\n256: - Do not replace DOM events, storage, observers, viewports, layout methods, pointer, or drag APIs unless the browser genuinely lacks one.\r\n257: - Prefer real nodes, events, styles/layout, and observers.\r\n258: - Centralize event factories: `createPointerEvent`, `createDragEvent`, `typeInput`, `fireTransitionEnd`.\r\n259: - Centralize DOM builders: `createButtonElement`, `createDropdownElements`, `createModalElement`.\r\n260: - Assert DOM state, emitted events, callback records, focus, classes, attributes, and public API state.\r\n261: - Do not assert private state, internal timers, or framework scheduler internals.\r\n262: - Prefer real short timers and observable wakeups. Never replace the host clock.\r\n263: \r\n264: ## Runner configuration\r\n265: \r\n266: Keep Vitest/provider configuration minimal:\r\n267: \r\n268: - Prefer defaults until a measured problem proves them insufficient.\r\n269: - Centralize provider setup in one helper/shared block.\r\n270: - Add browser/provider/teardown/timeout/parallelism/cache/launch settings only for a current verified need.\r\n271: - Avoid long browser flag lists and persistent contexts unless a test requires them.\r\n272: - For slow teardown, inspect test cleanup, open handles, file parallelism, and context churn before adding launch flags.\r\n273: - Remove exploratory settings after fixing the cause.\r\n274: - Config comments explain the current reason, not the history of failed experiments.\r\n275: \r\n276: ## Untestable usually means missing seam\r\n277: \r\n278: Before accepting that a behavior cannot be tested, look for the seam that would make it testable.\r\n279: \r\n280: - Treat a collaborator reached through a hard-coded global - a stream, a clock source, a spawn, a fetch - as a missing injection point, not an untestable truth.\r\n281: - An injected collaborator with a real minimal implementation is a sanctioned boundary stub, not a mock of project-owned behavior.\r\n282: - Add the seam rather than shipping the gap whenever the design would welcome it anyway, and whenever a sibling collaborator is already injected.\r\n283: - Record a genuinely irreducible gap where a reader meets it: what is unproven, why it cannot be driven, and what would change that. A silent untested guard reads exactly like a tested one.\r\n284: \r\n285: Coverage rules:\r\n286: \r\n287: - Read a coverage report as a discovery input, never as evidence of proof. It answers one cheap mechanical question - which code no test executed - and that reliably finds forgotten branches and rules nothing calls.\r\n288: - Never cite coverage as the adequacy audit's result. It cannot tell you whether an executed line is asserted, so a fully covered file can still be entirely unproven.\r\n289: - Never let a percentage become the target.\r\n290: \r\n291: ## Discovery and adequacy audit\r\n292: \r\n293: Before acceptance:\r\n294: \r\n295: - prove every intended test file is discovered by the correct project;\r\n296: - prove every declared project is reachable from a gate. A project registered in the root\r\n297:   configuration with no script, or with a script no chain runs, is a proof that never executes - and\r\n298:   because it never executes it never fails, so the suite reports green while carrying it. Read the\r\n299:   chain, not the exit code: run each project directly once and compare that list against what `test`\r\n300:   actually invokes. The gate that would report this gap is the gate that is missing.\r\n301: - prove a declared project's include resolves to a real file. An empty project is not a passing\r\n302:   project: Vitest exits non-zero on \"no test files found\", so a project aimed at a path that was\r\n303:   never created stays invisible until something finally runs it.\r\n304: - inspect actual test counts and environments;\r\n305: - audit `.todo`, `.skip`, conditional skips, retries, and inflated timeouts;\r\n306: - confirm each assertion would fail for the defect it claims to catch, and that it fails rather than passes when its population is empty;\r\n307: - confirm helpers do not reimplement production behavior;\r\n308: - confirm cleanup runs after setup or assertion failure;\r\n309: - confirm current-scope requirements have real tests rather than placeholders.\r\nscaffold/.claude/rules/workspace.md\r\n1: ---\r\n2: paths:\r\n3:   - 'src/**/*'\r\n4:   - 'app/**/*'\r\n5:   - 'tests/**/*'\r\n6:   - 'configs/**/*'\r\n7:   - 'demo/**/*'\r\n8:   - 'package.json'\r\n9:   - 'tsconfig.json'\r\n10:   - 'vite.config.ts'\r\n11: ---\r\n12: \r\n13: # Workspace, environments, builds, and scripts\r\n14: \r\n15: Use only the environments a project needs, and keep the root dependency model intact while doing it.\r\n16: \r\n17: ## Environments\r\n18: \r\n19: | Path           | Purpose                                                       |\r\n20: | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |\r\n21: | `src/core/`    | Published host-independent library                            |\r\n22: | `src/browser/` | Published browser-only library                                |\r\n23: | `src/server/`  | Published Node-only library                                   |\r\n24: | `src/styles/`  | Optional SCSS bundle producing `index.css`                    |\r\n25: | `src/bin/`     | Optional executable; `main.ts` entry, never a public barrel   |\r\n26: | `app/core/`    | Shared application logic with an `index.ts` barrel            |\r\n27: | `app/browser/` | Browser app; `main.ts` entry, not a barrel                    |\r\n28: | `app/server/`  | Node server app; `main.ts` entry                              |\r\n29: | `tests/`       | Mirrors src/app environments; root holds cross-cutting proofs |\r\n30: | `configs/`     | Thin target wrappers around root configs                      |\r\n31: \r\n32: - Dependency direction is the root project model in `AGENTS.md` and is not restated here; this file governs where the environments live and how they are configured.\r\n33: - Typical browser-app domains: `components/`, `pages/`, `composables/`, `controllers/`, `services/`, `stores/`.\r\n34: - Typical server-app domains: `handlers.ts`, `middlewares.ts`, `routes.ts`.\r\n35: - `src/styles/index.ts` is a side-effect entry importing `./index.scss`.\r\n36: - `src/bin/main.ts` is the executable entry, built to `dist/bin/main.js`. The name is fixed, as it\r\n37:   is for `app/browser/main.ts` and `app/server/main.ts`, so every runtime entry in a workspace is\r\n38:   found at the same name.\r\n39: - `package.json`'s `bin` key is the installed command name. The entry path is the value and does\r\n40:   not carry that name.\r\n41: \r\n42: ## Aliases\r\n43: \r\n44: | Alias          | Target                 |\r\n45: | -------------- | ---------------------- |\r\n46: | `@src/core`    | `src/core/index.ts`    |\r\n47: | `@src/browser` | `src/browser/index.ts` |\r\n48: | `@src/server`  | `src/server/index.ts`  |\r\n49: | `@src/styles`  | `src/styles/index.ts`  |\r\n50: | `@app/core`    | `app/core/index.ts`    |\r\n51: | `@app/browser` | `app/browser/index.ts` |\r\n52: | `@app/server`  | `app/server/index.ts`  |\r\n53: \r\n54: Define aliases in `tsconfig.json` first. `vite.config.ts` derives from `compilerOptions.paths`; keep both aligned.\r\n55: \r\n56: ## Configuration authority\r\n57: \r\n58: - `tsconfig.json`: shared compiler options, all-tree types, and path aliases.\r\n59: - `vite.config.ts`: shared builds, test projects, environment loading/mapping, and aliases.\r\n60: - `*/types.ts`: public API contracts.\r\n61: - `configs/src/` and `configs/app/`: thin per-target wrappers, including optional\r\n62:   `configs/src/*bin*` files. Shared logic remains in root configs.\r\n63: - `configs/helpers.ts`, `configs/browsers.ts`, and `configs/policy.ts`: the only permitted leaves\r\n64:   under `configs/`. Each imports nothing from the workspace, which is what keeps it a leaf, so no\r\n65:   `configs/types.ts` exists for one to import: each keeps its own types, data, and functions in its\r\n66:   one file, and the centralized-kind placement in `.claude/rules/architecture.md` does not reach a\r\n67:   leaf. Each `configs/src/*.config.ts` imports the root config rather than a leaf, so shared build\r\n68:   logic stays in one place.\r\n69: - Keep `configs/helpers.ts` free of any dependency a core-only workspace does not declare. It is\r\n70:   vendored byte-identical to every workspace, so an import there must resolve in all of them.\r\n71:   `configs/browsers.ts` exists for that reason: it imports `playwright` and\r\n72:   `@vitest/browser-playwright`, and only a workspace with a browser environment is given it.\r\n73: - Keep `configs/policy.ts` free of imports entirely. It is the workspace's oxlint plugin, the lint\r\n74:   instrument of the policy law, and it is vendored byte-identical to every workspace including a\r\n75:   core-only one, so a module that imports nothing at all is the only form that resolves in all of\r\n76:   them.\r\n77: - When a file is vendored byte-identical, import only what resolves in every workspace: a `node:`\r\n78:   module, or a package `BASE_DEV_DEPENDENCIES` declares. Refuse any other `@orkestrel/*` import;\r\n79:   `tests/src/server/helpers.test.ts` reads every vendored JavaScript and TypeScript module against\r\n80:   that set. A base package resolves in its own checkout through its `exports` map to its built\r\n81:   `dist/` entry, so a vendored module that imports it runs there after `npm run build`; the\r\n82:   generated root `tsconfig.json` maps the workspace's own published specifiers to its source, so\r\n83:   `npm run check` there needs no build.\r\n84: \r\n85: Environment rules:\r\n86: \r\n87: - `vite.config.ts` owns environment loading/mapping.\r\n88: - Add shared variables there first.\r\n89: - Prefer a minimal plain set such as `APP_NAME`, `APP_API_PATH`, `APP_HOST`, `APP_PORT`.\r\n90: - Expose extra browser runtime values only for a concrete need.\r\n91: \r\n92: ## Build outputs\r\n93: \r\n94: | Output             | Content                        | Format          |\r\n95: | ------------------ | ------------------------------ | --------------- |\r\n96: | `dist/src/core`    | Core library + declarations    | ES and CJS      |\r\n97: | `dist/src/browser` | Browser library + declarations | ES              |\r\n98: | `dist/src/server`  | Server library + declarations  | ES and CJS      |\r\n99: | `dist/src/styles`  | Compiled `index.css`           | ES wrapper      |\r\n100: | `dist/bin`         | Optional executable `main.js`  | ES with shebang |\r\n101: | `dist/app/browser` | Browser application            | target-defined  |\r\n102: | `dist/app/server`  | Server application             | CJS             |\r\n103: | `dist/showcase`    | Single-file `index.html` demo  | self-contained  |\r\n104: \r\n105: - Build\r\n100:   any example a reader executes with `pathToFileURL`.\r\nscaffold/.claude/rules/quality.md\r\n1: ---\r\n2: paths:\r\n3:   - 'src/**/*'\r\n4:   - 'app/**/*'\r\n5:   - 'tests/**/*'\r\n6:   - 'guides/**/*'\r\n7:   - 'package.json'\r\n8:   - 'vite.config.ts'\r\n9:   - 'tsconfig.json'\r\n10:   - '.agents/skills/**/*'\r\n11:   - '.claude/skills/**/*'\r\n12: ---\r\n13: \r\n14: # Research, hardening, and completion rules\r\n15: \r\n16: ## Evidence before change\r\n17: \r\n18: - Research when the user asks for it, when comparing an upstream, protocol, or legacy implementation, or when current external behavior materially affects design.\r\n19: - Use current primary sources for external capabilities, and the exact installed declarations and guides for dependencies. Separate verified fact from inference.\r\n20: - Read authoritative types and named decision-bearing implementation files first-hand. Delegate bulk supporting context, never the owning design decision.\r\n21: - Treat existing code, tests, `old/`, branches, and copied projects as evidence, not authority.\r\n22: - Build a capability/defect matrix before a broad API or production-readiness change. Every row ends as implement, repair, retain, or intentionally exclude with evidence.\r\n23: - Fix that matrix when the change starts. It is the definition of done, and the change closes when every row closes.\r\n24: - Never end a row as \"hardened further.\" Replace any evaluative phrase with the concrete condition that closes the row.\r\n25: - Record a finding outside the matrix against the row that owns it, for the next matrix. Do not reopen this one.\r\n26: \r\n27: ## Probes before arguments\r\n28: \r\n29: A question a probe can settle is settled by the probe, whether or not anyone has disputed it. Reasoning decides what to run and what the result means. It does not replace the run.\r\n30: \r\n31: - Test your own assumptions before you rely on them. You do not need a disagreement to justify a probe. If you are about to depend on what a function returns, what a config resolves to, what a flag does, or whether a path is even reached, run it and find out.\r\n32: - Treat a long deliberation about behaviour as the signal to stop and run something. Deliberation that a ten-line probe would have ended is the most expensive habit in this process, and it is invisible because it feels like rigour.\r\n33: - Verify a belief before stating it, or label it as unverified. An unverified assertion put into context becomes a fact for everything downstream, including other agents, and correcting it later costs more than the check would have.\r\n34: - Hold a claim you issue to the standard you hold a claim you receive. Nothing downstream re-checks an instruction, so an unverified fact inside one becomes the premise of every task built on it. Auditing every report you receive while exempting every brief you write is the common form of this failure.\r\n35: - Prefer the check over the chain of reasoning whenever the check is cheap. Reading the installed declaration, running one line, or counting the call sites beats three paragraphs inferring the same thing, and it produces evidence you can hand to someone else.\r\n36: - Write the probe before the argument gets long. The moment a claim about behaviour is disputed - between engines, between a report and a rule, or in your own head - stop and run it. Get the smallest real input through the real code and read the real output.\r\n37: - Bound the search before starting it, and put the bound in the brief. Name the benchmark, the population, or the row that ends it. An investigation with no stated stopping condition runs until attention runs out. This includes the case where the honest answer is that the limit is inherent and belongs in documentation rather than in code.\r\n38: - Treat a negative probe as evidence about the probe until its input is shown to reach the code under test. A pass proves nothing if the vector never arrived. Instrument the path, assert an observable side effect, or drive it through a door you can see.\r\n39: - When a report names a defect and your reproduction comes back clean, assume first that your vector was weaker than theirs, and go get their exact vector. Treating a failed reproduction as a disproof is the most common way a true finding is lost.\r\n40: - A reported vector the compiler rejects refutes the VECTOR, never the finding. Where a claim asserts reachability through a typed API, compile the exact vector under the project's own settings; re-derive one the types admit before dropping the finding, and record which vector was actually tested.\r\n41: - Reproduce a reported defect's cause before instructing a fix from it. A real symptom can carry a wrong diagnosis, and a fix aimed at the stated cause edits the wrong file while the defect survives.\r\n42: - Do not read a result into a tool's failure to find your probe. \"No tests found\", an empty match, a skipped file, a runner that resolved nothing - these report on the harness, not the subject. Confirm the probe was collected and executed first.\r\n43: - Prefer an observation over a derivation, including your own. When a measurement and an argument disagree, the argument is wrong until the measurement is shown to be broken.\r\n44: - Diagnose from the artifact the work produces - the file, the count, the exit code, the timestamp on what changed - never from a wrapper or a proxy signal that merely correlates with progress. Read a gate bare: a pipeline stage after it (`| tail`, `| grep`) reports the stage's exit status and hides the gate's failing lines.\r\n45: - Verify a comment or an agent's report against the call sites before relying on it. A code comment is not evidence. When lanes disagree about whether a path is live, count the callers rather than weighing the prose.\r\n46: - What a round proves is what it ran. A conclusion carried from one door to another is a hypothesis at the second door. Re-run it there.\r\n47: \r\n48: ## Falsification\r\n49: \r\n50: A review that reads a diff finds what the diff shows. A review that tries to break named claims finds what the diff hides. Code that has passed diff review several times can still carry a defect nobody has tried to trigger.\r\n51: \r\n52: ### Writing the claims\r\n53: \r\n54: - State the subject as a numbered list of the claims the work makes, never as \"review this diff.\" Each claim is falsifiable: a property some concrete input, state, or interleaving could show false.\r\n55: - Instruct the auditor to attempt refutation, not confirmation. A claim it cannot break is CONFIRMED with the evidence that convinced it. A claim it breaks is BROKEN with the exact failing input, state, or interleaving, plus the smallest correct fix.\r\n56: - Derive claims from what the change asserts under adverse conditions: cancellation, restart, concurrency, partial failure, hostile input, resource exhaustion, and the orderings a happy path never reaches.\r\n57: - Read the installed declaration or implementation of every substrate a claim depends on. A claim about `stop()` is unfalsifiable until you know what `stop()` does when the status is not the one the caller assumed.\r\n58: \r\n59: ### Instruments\r\n60: \r\n61: - An instrument is not evidence until it has failed. Pair every probe, comparison, or matrix with a negative control that must report failure, run under the same conditions. An identity check whose control reports \"same\" has measured nothing.\r\n62: - When a question about a TypeScript edit can supply a workspace project, a case of workspace files with a test, and a negative control naming its files, its test, the stage it must fail at, and why, call the `prove` tool the `probe` MCP server registers before relying on the answer. When the question supplies no project, no case, or no control, follow `.claude/rules/tests.md` \u0015 Probes and report the fallback instrument's own control and coverage.\r\n63: - When no `probe` server is registered in the session, register one outside the repository, in the harness's own local or user MCP scope - in Claude Code, `claude mcp add` outside project scope - naming the installed `node_modules/@orkestrel/probe/dist/bin/main.js` entry, and start it in the repository whose projects the question names, because the server fixes its workspace from its own working directory. The registration cannot live in the tree: a scaffold target holds no `.mcp.json` file, that path is instruction canon, and a copy at it reports as foreign drift on every `scaffold audit` run. Where the harness registers no server at all, treat the question as supplying no project and take the preceding rule's fallback.\r\n64: - Quote the closing line of the `prove` answer verbatim in every report, brief, and audit verdict that rests on the claim: the `receipt probe:<digest>:.` line when the case ran clean and the control broke exactly where the claim declared it would, and the `no receipt` line otherwise. A `no receipt` line leaves the claim unproved - report it with the stage that refused.\r\n65: - Read a receipt as evidence about its claim, never as a gate result. The gate chain still runs, and `verifier` still owns its result.\r\n66: - Draw the negative control from outside the population the instrument covers. Name the instrument's membership rule first, then pick a control that rule excludes. A control sampled from constructs the instrument already handles proves only that it discriminates among those constructs, and says nothing about the class it silently cannot reach.\r\n67: - State an instrument's coverage beside its result. A conclusion inherits the instrument's scope, not the question's. An unstated coverage claim is read as complete, and it never is. A search proves something about the paths it walked, so name them.\r\n68: - Match the instrument to the question. A text search reports on text, so a claim about declarations, call sites, or structure needs the compiler or a parser instead. A pattern written for one spelling of a construct reports on that spelling alone. A path check answers relative to the directory it runs from, so resolve the inputs against their own base before reading a miss as a finding.\r\n69: - Name the rival reading the instrument must exclude, and show it reports differently under that reading. Give independent measurements independent state: one counter shared across members reports read order and per-member read count identically, so a result consistent with both measured neither.\r\n70: - Report a question unanswered rather than answering it with a weaker instrument. A fallback that measures something adjacent returns a confident wrong answer, and nothing downstream can tell that answer from the real one - searching commit messages for a release when the question is where a version changed will match some release, but not the one asked about. Name the substitute and what it actually measures, or say the question is open.\r\n71: - State what the controls established and what they did not. An instrument certified only from the inside is trusted exactly where it has never been tested.\r\n72: - Treat a gap between what an instrument says it checks and what it actually matches as a defect in the instrument, not as a documented limit. A recorded blind spot buys trust only when everything outside it is genuinely covered.\r\n73: - Measure the product, not the harness. A recorded baseline that counts something about its own fixture is not evidence about the shipped surface, however often a guide quotes it.\r\n74: - Baseline a published-artifact claim against the published artifact. \"Did my change move the surface\" and \"does this release differ from the last one\" are different questions, and a diff against your own starting point answers only the first. A toolchain that re-emits declarations moves the artifact without any source edit, so every writer can correctly report an unmoved surface while the package's published contract has changed. Fetch what consumers actually have - the tarball, the deployed asset - and compare against that.\r\n75: - Prove a module cycle by loading the built artifact, not by a green suite. Tests import through the source graph and a bundler resolves it differently, so a cycle that is fatal at module-init in the shipped form can stay invisible under every test. Import each published entry point and read an export from it.\r\n76: - Adopt an instrument that settled a claim as a test before accepting the work it settled. The probe that proved a fix, carrying the control that proved the probe, is that fix's regression guard. A verification that runs once is a rehearsal, not a gate.\r\n77: \r\n78: ### Rounds and verdicts\r\n79: \r\n80: - Treat an all-confirmed round as a legitimate result, and put the brief on trial rather than the subject. Re-read the claims and ask whether any could have been falsified by evidence the round actually had. If none could, the claims were descriptive and the round proved nothing - sharpen them and re-run. If they could have been and were not, the pass stands.\r\n81: - Name the claims you could not break either way, so the next round knows what has already been attacked.\r\n82: - Never tell an auditor that a clean round means it did not try. That instructs it to manufacture a finding, and a manufactured finding costs a fix unit, an argument, and the credibility of the true findings beside it.\r\n83: - Treat a repaired claim as a new claim, not a settled one. Re-ask it at every entry point that reaches the same rule, not only the door the defect arrived through. The engine that wrote the fix is least able to see this, because re-verifying where the fix is feels like verifying the fix.\r\n84: - A fix that adopts the auditor's prescription verbatim may close with a mutation probe in place of a fresh audit round: disable the load-bearing line, watch the adopted pin fail, restore it, and commit the pin as the regression guard. A fix that departs from the prescription gets the cross-engine round.\r\n85: - Let reachability bound the fix. A defect reachable through the package's own shipped code or a documented extension seam falsifies its claim and is repaired now.\r\n86: - Document the obligation instead when a defect is reachable only through a hypothetical foreign implementation of a contract this package publishes. State it on the interface that owns it and prove the documentation. Do not build coordination machinery against a requirement nobody wrote down. Attacks are unlimited; reachable ones are not, and only the reachable set is a work list.\r\n87: - **Three rounds at one seam is the budget, and reaching it switches the search strategy rather than stopping the work.** Repeated rounds against one seam are evidence about the design, not evidence of diligence. At the third round, name what the audit is trying to accomplish, then pick the successor strategy from what the recurrence shows.\r\n88: - Recurrence with a direction - each fix relocates the class along one stream, or the evidence points up a dependency chain - ends the depth search. Run one breadth round that probes the stream's stations in parallel to locate the source, in the shape `.agents/orchestration.md` \u0015 Context and decomposition prescribes, then plan the downstream work from the source and size it by the sweep's map.\r\n89: - Recurrence with no direction makes the seam itself the question. The next unit is a ruling - on the threat model, the mechanism, or the boundary - taken with the same adversarial pass a design gets, not a fourth repair.\r\n90: - A subject that reprices itself on every edit - a count, a census, a total over prose - has no closing condition and is not a seam. Drop the claim, or recast it as the property the tally stood in for.\r\n91: - Write the round count down in the capability/defect matrix row that owns the seam, when the seam opens, so it is a fact rather than a feeling. A seam that has consumed more rounds than the rest of the matrix combined has already answered the question.\r\n92: - State the ruling that ends a seam as the invariant the code will obey, the constraint bounding it against over-correction, and the interface where a consumer meets the obligation. A ruling that names only the defect it replaces produces the opposite defect next round.\r\n93: - Give every behavioural audit the means to run its attacks. An auditor that cannot execute cannot falsify a behavioural claim: it returns derivations, and a derivation reads exactly like a verdict while being a different thing - it will confirm a claim one probe would break. Treat a report with no executed evidence as a review of the source, and label it as such.\r\n94: \r\n95: ## Ecosystem reuse\r\n96: \r\n97: The root laws on inspecting declared `@orkestrel/*` capabilities, reusing a matching primitive, and updating every consumer without shims bind here without restatement. A\r\n55:  *   missing / malformed field degrades to a sensible default (empty content, no\r\n56:  *   usage, `{}` arguments), never a throw.\r\n57:  * - **Bounded.** Each call arms a {@link Timeout} for `OllamaOptions.timeout` and\r\n58:  *   passes `AbortSignal.any([timeout.signal, signal])` to `fetch`, so the caller's\r\n59:  *   signal and the deadline both cancel the request. The timeout is always cleared -\r\n60:  *   in `#fetch` if the request fails/aborts, otherwise in the consuming call's `finally`.\r\n61:  * - **Abort recovers partial.** A `stream` cancelled mid-flight throws a\r\n62:  *   `ProviderAbortError` carrying the partial result assembled so far; pairing the\r\n63:  *   `TextDecoder({ stream: true })` with the `createNDJSONParser` parser keeps multi-byte\r\n64:  *   UTF-8 splits and partial lines honest.\r\n65:  * - **Event-free.** A pure functional boundary - no Emitter, no events.\r\n66:  * - **Transport seam.** {@link OllamaOptions.fetch} swaps the transport (default\r\n67:  *   `globalThis.fetch`) and {@link OllamaOptions.headers} is a per-request, possibly\r\n68:  *   async header injector merged over the base `Content-Type` - so a browser runtime\r\n69:  *   can route through the developer's own server with an obfuscated bearer token,\r\n70:  *   without this library ever handling a real API key. Both omitted ? the global `fetch`\r\n71:  *   and only a JSON content type.\r\n72:  *   Orthogonal to the deadline: the hook is awaited inside `#fetch`'s try, so a hook\r\n73:  *   rejection clears the armed timer like any other request failure.\r\n74:  *\r\n75:  * @example\r\n76:  * ```ts\r\n77:  * const provider = new OllamaProvider({ model: 'qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M' })\r\n78:  * const result = await provider.generate(messages, abort.signal)\r\n79:  * ```\r\n80:  */\r\n81: export class OllamaProvider implements ProviderInterface {\r\n82: \treadonly name = 'ollama'\r\n83: \treadonly #id: string\r\n84: \treadonly #model: string\r\n85: \treadonly #url: string\r\n86: \treadonly #keepAlive: string | number\r\n87: \treadonly #timeout: number\r\n88: \treadonly #think: boolean\r\n89: \treadonly #options: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>> | undefined\r\n90: \treadonly #transport: typeof globalThis.fetch\r\n91: \treadonly #headers:\r\n92: \t\t| (() => Readonly<Record<string, string>> | Promise<Readonly<Record<string, string>>>)\r\n93: \t\t| undefined\r\n94: \treadonly #format: ContextFormat | undefined\r\n95: \r\n96: \tconstructor(options: OllamaOptions) {\r\n97: \t\tthis.#id = crypto.randomUUID()\r\n98: \t\tthis.#model = options.model\r\n99: \t\tthis.#url = options.url ?? Every `unknown` wire value is narrowed through the `@orkestrel/contract` guards (`isRecord`, `isString`, `isNumber`) rather than a type assertion, and a missing or malformed field degrades to a sensible default (empty content, no usage, `{}` arguments) rather than a throw.\r\n9: \r\n10: Every call is bounded by the caller's `AbortSignal` (a cancel, a deadline, or a budget, folded through `AbortSignal.any`) together with the provider's own armed `Timeout`; a `stream` cancelled mid-flight throws a `ProviderAbortError` (from `@orkestrel/agent`) carrying the partial. A per-call `ProviderStreamOptions.schema` (a JSON schema object, from `@orkestrel/agent`) forwards verbatim as the wire's structured-output `format` field, and is omitted from the request when no schema is supplied. Each takes the conversation, a bounding `AbortSignal`, optional `tools`, and optional per-call `ProviderStreamOptions`.\r\n99: \r\n100: | Method     | Returns                                         | Summary                                                                                                                                                      |\r\n101: | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |\r\n102: | `generate` | `Promise<ProviderResult>`                       | Generates one complete turn and resolves the assembled result - the clean content, any separated reasoning, any tool calls, and any usage the wire reported. |\r\n103: | `stream`   | `AsyncGenerator<ProviderDelta, ProviderResult>` | Streams one turn, yielding a channel-tagged delta per non-empty content or reasoning span and returning the assembled result when the stream completes.      |\r\n104: \r\n105: ## Contract\r\n106: \r\n107: These invariants hold across `src/server` \u001d `ollama.md` (the `ProviderInterface` / `ProviderResult` / `ProviderAbortError` contract itself is in `@orkestrel/agent`):\r\n108: \r\n109: 1. **Doc \u001d source bijection.** Every `function` / `class` / `const` / `interface` / `type` row in the `## Surface` table is a real export of the `src/server` surface, and every export appears as a Surface row - exhaustive, both directions.\r\n110: 2. **Imports each boundary from its owner, no cycle.** `OllamaProvider` implements `ProviderInterface` and throws `ProviderAbortError`; those symbols, `Message`, and the provider result/delta/options shapes come from `@orkestrel/agent`. `ToolCall` / `ToolDefinition` come from `@orkestrel/tool`, `TokenUsage` from `@orkestrel/budget`, the `NDJSONParser` from `@orkestrel/ndjson`, the `Timeout` from `@orkestrel/timeout`, and the `@orkestrel/contract` guards (`isRecord` / `isString` / `isNumber`) from `@orkestrel/contract`. Each dependency is one-way and never imports from `@src/server`.\r\n111: 3. **The `/api/chat` wire protocol.** `OllamaProvider` POSTs `{ model, messages, stream, keep_alive, think }` to `${url}/api/chat` (the `think` flag is the per-call `ProviderStreamOptions.think` override when present, else `OllamaOptions.think`, default `false`), adding `options` only when configured and `tools` only when a non-empty `ToolDefinition[]` is passed. Each tool maps to `{ type: 'function', function: { name } }`, with `description` and `parameters` added only when the corresponding `ToolDefinition` fields are supplied. Messages map to the wire's minimal `{ role, content }` turn, with `tool_calls` added only on an assistant turn that replays them. A non-OK HTTP status throws `OllamaHTTPError('Ollama API error: <status> - <body>', status)`, its message bounded to a `2048`-char body excerpt (a body-read failure itself throws `OllamaHTTPError` with `'(error body unavailable)'` and a `cause`); a `stream` whose response arrives with a `null` body throws `OllamaHTTPError('Ollama API error: no response body', 0)`. Every throw carries `code: 'HTTP'`, so a caller branches on `error.code` and reads `error.status` for the HTTP number (`0` for the null-body case); `isOllamaHTTPError` narrows a caught value without parsing the message.\r\n112: 4. **Configurable `think` on the wire; the splitter keeps the assembled content clean.** For a thinking-capable model (for example `qwen3`) the per-request `think` flag is the only wire-level reasoning control (its native renderer honours neither the qwen3 `/no_think` token nor a Modelfile `PARAMETER think false`). It is configurable through `OllamaOptions.think` (default `false` - so the general-purpose provider stays immediate for non-thinking models and tests fast) and overrideable per call through `ProviderStreamOptions.think`. Set `think: true` when the caller displays reasoning separately from the answer. With `think: true` the daemon separates reasoning natively, returning it on the distinct `message.thinking` channel (yielded live as `ProviderDelta` `{ channel: 'thinking', text }` and accumulated onto `ProviderResult.thinking`) rather than inline in `message.content`. Either way the per-call `ThinkSplitter` (`createThinkSplitter` - fresh per stream) is the defensive fallback: a daemon may still ignore `think: false` for a thinking model and render reasoning inline as `<think>.</think>` content, so each call routes every content delta through the splitter - the assembled `content` is its authoritative clean accumulation (a tag split across NDJSON chunks is held until disambiguated, an unclosed span at stream end is treated as reasoning, and the qwen3 template's implicit pre-seeded open - a bare `</think>` with no open on the wire - reclassifies the surfaced prefix into thinking), and the separated spans - joined with any daemon-side `message.thinking` deltas - surface as `ProviderResult.thinking`, present only when non-empty. The reasoning never re-enters the conversation.\r\n113: 5. **Non-stream vs. NDJSON stream.** `generate` sends `stream: false` and parses one JSON body. `stream` sends `stream: true` and consumes NDJSON - one JSON object per `\\n`-terminated line - pairing a `TextDecoder({ stream: true })` (partial multi-byte characters) with the `@orkestrel/ndjson` `NDJSONParser` parser (partial lines) so a record split across byte reads is reassembled. Each delta line may carry `message.content` (split and yielded as a `content` delta when non-empty) and / or `message.thinking` (yielded as a `thinking` delta when non-empty); the final `done: true` line carries the token usage. At stream end the decoder's held multi-byte tail is flushed and fed through the parser (with a trailing `\\n` appended when non-empty) so a non-conformant proxy's final unterminated `done` line is still recovered rather than silently dropped; a `generate`'s non-stream body that is empty or fails to parse as a JSON record yields `undefined`, which the call site reads as `{}` (empty content, no usage), never a raw `SyntaxError` escaping to the caller.\r\n114: 6. **`stream` yields deltas + returns the assembled result.** The generator yields each non-empty clean content delta as `{ channel: 'content', text }` and each daemon-side reasoning delta as `{ channel: 'thinking', text }`; its return value is the assembled `ProviderResult` whose `content` is the splitter's authoritative clean accumulation - exactly the concatenation of the yielded content deltas (a held partial tag the stream never completed is yielded as the final content delta, so the equality holds), except across an implicit-open reclassification (the implicit-open case: the reasoning prefix had already streamed before the bare `</think>` revealed it, so the result drops it and the yields cannot be recalled) - plus any tool calls collected across lines, the usage from the `done` line, and the separated `thinking` when the turn produced any.\r\n115: 7. **Usage from the `done` line / body (reuses `TokenUsage`).** `ProviderResult.usage` is present only when both `prompt_eval_count` and `eval_count` are numbers on the parsed record (the non-stream body, or the stream's `done: true` line) - mapped to `{ prompt, completion, total: prompt + completion }`, the `TokenUsage` shape (imported, not redefined). A delta line carries neither count, so it contributes no usage.\r\n116: 8. **Tool-call extraction with id-generation (no `as`).** `result.tools` is the model's `message.tool_calls`, each entry narrowed to `{ id, name, arguments }`: the entry and its `function` must be records and `name` a string (else the entry is dropped); `arguments` is the wire object as-is, a JSON string parsed to a record, or `{}` when neither; `id` is the wire's `id` when a string, else a freshly minted `crypto.randomUUID()`. An empty result `tools` is never surfaced - its absence means \"no calls\".\r\n117: 9. **Boundary narrowing - all wire `unknown` through guards, never `as`.** Every value read off the wire (the parsed body, each NDJSON record, `message`, `content`, the usage counts, `tool_calls`, `arguments`) arrives as `unknown` and is narrowed through the `@orkestrel/contract` guards (`isRecord` / `isString` / `isNumber`) - never a type assertion. A missing or malformed field degrades to a sensible default (empty content, no usage, `{}` arguments), never a throw - the one external boundary kept honest.\r\n118: 10. **Bounded by an `AbortSignal` + a deadline.** Each call arms a `Timeout` for `OllamaOptions.timeout` (default `120_000`ms) and passes `AbortSignal.any([timeout.signal, callerSignal])` to `fetch`, so the caller's signal and the deadline both cancel the request; the timeout is always cleared - when the request fails or aborts, and otherwise after the response is consumed (never left armed). An already-aborted signal rejects the call before any content streams.\r\n119: 11. **Abort \u001a `ProviderAbortError` with the partial.** A `stream` cancelled mid-flight (the caller's signal or the deadline) throws a `ProviderAbortError` whose `partial` is the `ProviderResult` assembled from whatever streamed so far - including the splitter's held partial tag, flushed into the partial's `content` before it is thrown, exactly as at normal stream end; `isProviderAbortError` (from `@orkestrel/agent`) narrows a caught value so the loop can recover the partial content. A non-abort error propagates unchanged. The reader is `cancel()`ed (not merely released, freeing the underlying HTTP connection; tolerated as a no-op on an already-done/errored reader) and the parser cleared, both in a `finally`.\r\n120: 12. **Transport seam (custom `fetch` + dynamic `headers`).** `OllamaOptions.fetch` swaps the transport (default `globalThis.fetch`, bound to its `globalThis` receiver - `globalThis.fetch.bind(globalThis)` - because invoking a bare reference through a field loses the `window` receiver and browsers throw `Illegal invocation`; node's fetch is receiver-agnostic) and `OllamaOptions.headers` is a per-request, possibly-async injector whose returned `Readonly<Record<string, string>>` is merged on top of the base `Content-Type` (the hook adds headers; it overrides `Content-Type` only by explicitly returning one). Both are optional - omitted ? the bound global `fetch` and only `Content-Type: application/json`. This lets a browser-side runtime route through the developer's own server with an obfuscated/generated bearer token the server validates: **your app never handles a real API key** - the real key lives only on that server; the `headers` hook supplies whatever short-lived token it expects. The hook is awaited inside the request path's `try`, so a hook rejection clears the armed deadline like any other failure (merged through `Object.entries`, no `as`).\r\n121: 13. **Context-framing `format` (provider-default cascade level, expose-only).** `OllamaOptions.format` is an optional `ContextFormat` (from `@orkestrel/agent`) - the provider's context-framing default, exposed as `provider.format` to satisfy the optional `ProviderInterface.format`. It is the provider-default level of `AgentContext`'s build cascade (beats the managers' built-in framing, beaten by a manager-options or per-item override; see `@orkestrel/agent`), read by the Agent when it assembles the prompt. Omitted ? `undefined` (framing-agnostic; core's built-in framing applies unchanged). It is **never sent on the `/api/chat` wire**: it is consumed by core, absent from the request `body`, and is unrelated to Ollama's structured-output `/api/chat` `format` parameter - that one is sent in the request `body`, but only when a per-call `ProviderStreamOptions.schema` is supplied (omitted otherwise) - the framing default and that wire parameter only share a word.\r\n122: 14. **Event-free.** A pure functional boundary - no Emitter, no events.\r\n123: 15. **Tested live against a real local Ollama (no `skipIf`).** The provider tests run against a real Ollama daemon - no mocks, only genuine third-party calls - model `qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M`, with `OLLAMA_HOST` / `OLLAMA_MODEL` overridable. Unlike the other surfaces, the dedicated `service` project requires the daemon: `tests/setupService.ts` throws a clear error if it is unreachable and warms the model (a `num_predict: 1` chat) before the suite, so the live tests run unconditionally (no `describe.skipIf`). The project runs serially (`fileParallelism: false`) with a 120s test/hook timeout so a cold load can't flake it; `keep_alive` keeps the model resident across files, and `bash scripts/ollama.sh` brings the daemon and model up before the battery in CI. Assertions are structural - they hold whatever wording a small model produces - and never pin exact output.\r\n124: 16. **Doc \u001d source method bijection.** The `## Methods` table lists exactly `OllamaProvider`'s public methods (`generate` / `stream`), and the class exposes exactly those - no more.\r\n125: \r\n126: ## Patterns\r\n127: \r\n128: ### `createOllama` + `generate`\r\n129: \r\n130: The dominant single-shot use: one prompt, one assembled result.\r\n131: \r\n132: ```ts\r\n133: import { createAbort } from '@orkestrel/abort'\r\n134: import { createOllama } from '@orkestrel/ollama'\r\n135: \r\n136: const provider = createOllama({ model: 'qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M', options: { temperature: 0 } })\r\n137: const abort = createAbort()\r\n138: const messages = [\r\n139: \t{ id: '1', role: 'user', content: 'Summarize the release notes for version 2.0.' },\r\n140: ] as const\r\n141: \r\n142: const result = await provider.generate(messages, abort.signal)\r\n143: console.log(result.content)\r\n144: if (result.usage) charge(result.usage) // fold into a token budget\r\n145: ```\r\n146: \r\n147: ### Bounding a call with a budget + timeout\r\n148: \r\n149: `generate` / `stream` take a plain `AbortSignal`, so fold an abort, a timeout, and a token budget into one bound through `AbortSignal.any` - whichever trips first cancels the call. This caller-side bound stacks on top of the provider's own armed deadline (`OllamaOptions.timeout`, default `120_000`ms): the request dies when either fires, so you get an external cancel/budget and a hard per-call ceiling for free.\r\n150: \r\n151: ```ts\r\n152: import { createAbort } from '@orkestrel/abort'\r\n153: import { createTimeout } from '@orkestrel/timeout'\r\n154: import { createTokenBudget } from '@orkestrel/budget'\r\n155: import { createOllama } from '@orkestrel/ollama'\r\n156: \r\n157: const provider = createOllama({ model: 'qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M' })\r\n158: const abort = createAbort() // external cancel\r\n159: const timeout = createTimeout({ ms: 30_000 }) // wall-clock deadline\r\n160: const budget = createTokenBudget({ max: 50_000, scope: 'total' }) // cost ceiling\r\n161: timeout.start()\r\n162: budget.start()\r\n163: \r\n164: const bound = AbortSignal.any([abort.signal, timeout.signal, budget.signal])\r\n165: const result = await provider.generate(messages, bound)\r\n166: budget.consume(result.usage ?? { prompt: 0, completion: 0, total: 0 })\r\n167: ```\r\n168: \r\n169: ### Routing through your own server (obfuscated tokens)\r\n170: \r\n171: In the browser you must not ship the real LLM API key. Instead, deploy a thin server that holds the real key, point the provider's `url` at that server, and use `headers` to attach a generated/obfuscated token your server validates before relaying the request to the real LLM. The custom `fetch` lets you swap the transport (for example a browser fetch, an instrumented wrapper) without touching the wire protocol. The client itself never handles the real API key - it only attaches the header your hook returns. Omitting the transport and the header hook leaves the global `fetch` and only `Content-Type: application/json`.\r\n172: \r\n173: ```ts\r\n174: import { createAbort } from '@orkestrel/abort'\r\n175: import { createOllama } from '@orkestrel/ollama'\r\n176: \r\n177: const provider = createOllama({\r\n178: \tmodel: 'qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M',\r\n179: \turl: 'https://my-app.example.com/llm', // your server, which forwards to the real LLM\r\n180: \theaders: async () => ({ authorization: `Bearer ${await mintToken()}` }), // server validates this\r\n181: \t// fetch: myFetch, // optional: inject a custom transport\r\n182: })\r\n183: const abort = createAbort()\r\n184: const result = await provider.generate(messages, abort.signal)\r\n185: ```\r\n186: \r\n187: The `headers` hook is called once per request (async, so a token can be refreshed each call); its result merges on top of the base `Content-Type`, so it adds an authorization header without disturbing the JSON body. The real key stays on your server - the client never sees it.\r\n188: \r\n189: ### Context framing\r\n190: \r\n191: `OllamaOptions.format` is the provider's context-framing default - a `ContextFormat` (from `@orkestrel/agent`) declaring how this provider's models prefer the context sections framed (for example XML group wrappers vs. Markdown headers). It is the **provider-default level** of `AgentContext`'s build cascade (see `@orkestrel/agent`): it beats the managers' built-in framing but is beaten by a manager-options or per-item override. `createOllama` accepts it directly and `OllamaProvider` exposes it as `provider.format`, satisfying the optional `ProviderInterface.format`; the Agent reads it when it assembles the prompt. Omit it and the provider is framing-agnostic - core's built-in section framing applies unchanged.\r\n192: \r\n193: ```ts\r\n194: import { createOllama } from '@orkestrel/ollama'\r\n195: \r\n196: const provider = createOllama({\r\n197: \tmodel: 'qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M',\r\n198: \tformat: {\r\n199: \t\tinstructions: {\r\n200: \t\t\topen: '<instructions>',\r\n201: \t\t\trender: (instruction) => `<instruction>${instruction.content}</instruction>`,\r\n202: \t\t\tclose: '</instructions>',\r\n203: \t\t},\r\n204: \t},\r\n205: })\r\n206: provider.format // the ContextFormat preceding - read by AgentContext.build()\r\n207: ```\r\n208: \r\n209: **Not the wire `format`.** This is the prompt-context framing consumed by `AgentContext.build()` - it is **expose-only** and is never sent on the `/api/chat` request. It is unrelated to Ollama's `/api/chat` `format` parameter (structured output / JSON schema): that wire field is driven by a different, per-call source - `ProviderStreamOptions.schema` (from `@orkestrel/agent`) - forwarded verbatim as `format` and omitted from the body when `schema` is undefined. The framing default and the wire parameter share a word and nothing else: the framing default is a hint the daemon never sees, and the wire parameter is a per-call constraint the provider never exposes back.\r\n210: \r\n211: ### Narrowing HTTP errors with `isOllamaHTTPError`\r\n212: \r\n213: Branch on the HTTP status rather than parsing the thrown message: narrow a caught value with `isOllamaHTTPError` and read `error.status`.\r\n214: \r\n215: ```ts\r\n216: import { createAbort } from '@orkestrel/abort'\r\n217: import { createOllama, isOllamaHTTPError } from '@orkestrel/ollama'\r\n218: \r\n219: const provider = createOllama({ model: 'qwen3.5:2b-q4_K_M' })\r\n220: const abort = createAbort()\r\n221: const messages = [{ id: '1', role: 'user', content: 'Reply with exactly: ok' }] as const\r\n222: \r\n223: try {\r\n224: \tawait provider.generate(messages, abort.signal)\r\n225: } catch (error) {\r\n226: \tif (isOllamaHTTPError(error) && error.status === 404) {\r\n227: \t\t// the configured model isn't pulled\r\n228: \t} else if (isOllamaHTTPError(error) && error.status === 400) {\r\n229: \t\t// malformed request (for example an empty model string)\r\n230: \t} else {\r\n231: \t\tthrow error\r\n232: \t}\r\n233: }\r\n234: ```\r\n235: \r\n236: ### Practices\r\n237: \r\n238: - **Import the contract from `@orkestrel/agent`, the provider from `@orkestrel/ollama`** - `ProviderInterface` / `ProviderResult` / `isProviderAbortError` live in `@orkestrel/agent`; `createOllama` / `OllamaProvider` / `OllamaOptions` live in `@orkestrel/ollama`.\r\n239: - **Import tool-call shapes from `@orkestrel/tool`** - `ToolDefinition` / `ToolCall` live with the tool runtime, while the provider contract that consumes them stays in `@orkestrel/agent`.\r\n240: - **Bound every call** - pass an `AbortSignal` (an abort, or an `AbortSignal.any` over abort + timeout + budget) so a request can be cancelled, deadlined, or capped.\r\n241: - **Recover the stream's partial** - wrap a driven `stream` in `try`/`catch` and narrow with `isProviderAbortError` to keep the content that arrived before a cancel.\r\n242: - **Branch on the HTTP status, not the message** - narrow a caught value with `isOllamaHTTPError` and read `error.status` (`404` for an unpulled model) instead of parsing `error.message`.\r\n243: - **Fold usage into a budget** - `result.usage` is the `TokenUsage` shape; `consume` it per turn to enforce a token ceiling.\r\n244: - **Give a thinking model headroom** - with `think: true`, a reasoning model (for example `qwen3.5:2b` at `temperature: 0`) can spend 200+ tokens on `message.thinking` before any `content` token arrives; a tight `num_predict` cap or a tight external token budget can exhaust before content starts, yielding empty `result.content` - and `@orkestrel/agent`'s budget enforcement can abort mid-stream with `partial: true` if the cap is hit while thinking is still draining it. Size `num_predict` / the budget with thinking overhead in mind for any model run with `think: true`.\r\n245: - **Tune through `options`** - pass sampling parameters (`temperature`, `seed`, and `num_predict`) through `OllamaOptions.options`; they forward verbatim to the wire.\r\n246: - **Observe at the call site** - the provider publishes no events; read `stream`'s deltas and its returned result for everything a turn produced.\r\n247: \r\n248: ## Tests\r\n249: \r\n250: - [`tests/guides.test.ts`](../tests/guides.test.ts) - the `## Surface` \u001d `src/server` bijection (value + type exports), the `OllamaProvider` method bijection, and the equality gate: every `Summary` cell against its declaration's description paragraph, the titled `createOllama + generate` fence against the `@example` block of that title (pinned so the titled pair cannot be retired silently), and the README pitch against this guide's tagline. A `Conversation` holds the history - a live tail of immutable messages plus the sections older turns were compacted into. An `AgentContext` assembles that history into the next prompt, folding in the instructions and the active workspace and applying the active scope. An `Agent` drives that prompt through a provider, dispatches whatever tools the model asks for, feeds the results back, and repeats until the model stops. Everything else in this module either configures those nouns or observes them. Source: [`src/core`](../src/core). Reasoning separation, the authority gate, and durable jobs sit around that boundary. The model itself is the one thing this package does not supply: `ProviderInterface` is a contract, not an implementation, so any backend that satisfies it drops in unchanged and the host application decides which one. Nor is there hidden global state, a plugin lifecycle, a prompt-template DSL, or an implicit memory store. This is a kit of composable primitives: the loop is the convenient way to use them, not the only one, and a caller that would rather bound and drive a provider by hand can skip it entirely.\r\n11: \r\n12: Tools and files are borrowed, not owned. Callable tools come from [`@orkestrel/tool`](tool.md): the loop advertises their definitions to the model, dispatches the calls that come back, and feeds each `ToolResult` in as a tool message. A tool is loop machinery - it is never rendered into the prompt. Documents come from [`@orkestrel/workspace`](workspace.md): the context renders the active workspace into every turn, split by carrier - text as fenced reference blocks in the system message, images attached to the last user turn. That split is this package's own product policy, decided here because only the prompt-assembly layer knows what a turn looks like.\r\n13: \r\n14: A turn is bounded and always terminates. One `AbortSignal` - a cancel, a [timeout](timeout.md), and a [budget](budget.md) folded together through `AbortSignal.any` - bounds the whole run, and tool iteration is capped at `limit`. A cancel is not an error: it commits a partial `AgentResult` that resolves, so only a genuine provider or tool failure rejects. `generate` and `stream` share one private run, so the one-shot result can never diverge from the live stream, and a buggy observer cannot corrupt either, because the emitter isolates a listener's throw.\r\n15: \r\n16: ## Surface\r\n17: \r\n18: The agent-owned surface: the inference boundary, the conversation layer, the context and its managers, the loop, the authority gate, and the durable-job bridge. Tool and workspace entities belong to their originating packages and are consumed directly - never re-exported here - and the concrete `ProviderInterface` implementation belongs to the host application.\r\n19: \r\n20: A provider turns a conversation (plus optional tools) into a turn: `generate` resolves the assembled `ProviderResult` (content + any tool calls + any usage); `stream` yields channel-tagged `ProviderDelta`s as they arrive (`content` for answer text, `thinking` for live reasoning) and returns the same assembled result when the stream completes, so a caller can render tokens / reasoning live and still get the full outcome. Both bound the call with an `AbortSignal`:\r\n21: \r\n22: ```ts\r\n23: import { createAbort } from '@orkestrel/abort'\r\n24: import type { ProviderInterface } from '@orkestrel/agent'\r\n25: \r\n26: declare const provider: ProviderInterface // any concrete implementation supplied by the host app\r\n27: const abort = createAbort()\r\n28: const messages = [{ id: '1', role: 'user', content: 'Say hello.' }] as const\r\n29: \r\n30: const result = await provider.generate(messages, abort.signal)\r\n31: result.content // the assembled content\r\n32: result.usage // { prompt, completion, total } - folds into a token budget\r\n33: \r\n34: const generator = provider.stream(messages, abort.signal)\r\n35: let step = await generator.next()\r\n36: while (!step.done) {\r\n37: \tif (step.value.channel === 'content') process.stdout.write(step.value.text)\r\n38: \tif (step.value.channel === 'thinking') process.stderr.write(step.value.text)\r\n39: \tstep = await generator.next()\r\n40: }\r\n41: const streamed = step.value // the assembled ProviderResult (content === the joined content deltas)\r\n42: ```\r\n43: \r\n44: Pass `tools` (a non-empty `ToolDefinition[]`) to advertise callable tools for the turn; when the model calls one, `result.tools` is a `ToolCall[]` (each with a guaranteed `id`, the tool `name`, and parsed `arguments`). Aborting a `stream` mid-flight throws a `ProviderAbortError` whose `partial` holds whatever streamed before the cancel.\r\n45: \r\n46: A tool is a JSON-Schema-described callable from [`@orkestrel/tool`](tool.md), and the loop needs exactly this from its registry: `definitions()` advertises the tools to the model, and `execute` dispatches the `ToolCall`s that come back. What returns is a `ToolResult` discriminated on `success` - an unknown name and a throwing handler both arrive as the failure arm rather than as an exception, and a batch isolates each call from its siblings, which is what lets the loop hand every outcome back to the model and let it react:\r\n47: \r\n48: ```ts\r\n378: ### Factories\r\n379: \r\n380: | API                               | Kind     | Summary                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |\r\n381: | --------------------------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\r\n382: | `createConversation`              | function | Creates a conversation -
